life-admin.name: Buried in paperwork
life-admin.line: I lose hours every week to forms, bills and waiting on hold.
life-admin.why: Keeps the original's forms and bills, swaps the British "phone queues" for the American "waiting on hold", and makes the name a problem like Busy and Legal trouble.

life-admin.name: Too much paperwork
life-admin.line: Forms, bills and calls on hold eat up my week.
life-admin.why: Keeps the original almost word for word in everyday American words, with a problem name that matches the rest of the heading.

chores.name: Too many chores
chores.line: I spend my days cooking and cleaning.
chores.why: The line is already plain and recognizable; only the name changes from an area to a problem, so the heading reads one way.

chores.name: Never-ending chores
chores.line: I finish the cooking and cleaning and it's time to start again.
chores.why: Says what makes chores a pain, that they never end, in words people use about their own day, and gives a problem name like Busy and Doomscrolling.

no-fun.name: No fun
no-fun.line: I can't remember the last time I did something just for fun.
no-fun.why: Keeps the original's feeling and says plainly that the missing thing is fun, not time, so it separates cleanly from Busy; the name becomes a problem.

no-fun.name: No fun
no-fun.line: I can't remember the last time I played.
no-fun.why: Keeps the original line and only changes the area name Fun into a problem name like Busy and Doomscrolling.

pairs.distinction: Busy is having no time of your own for any reason; Chores names one specific thing that eats the day.
pairs.reason: Someone whose time goes to cooking and cleaning will pick Chores, while someone stretched by work, commutes or everything at once picks Busy.

pairs.distinction: Busy is about hours; Burnout is about having no energy left, even with time.
pairs.reason: People can be short on time without being burned out, and burned out with free evenings, so the choice is easy.

pairs.distinction: Caregiving names looking after someone, which takes more than time; Busy is general.
pairs.reason: A caregiver recognizes their own pain in Caregiving at once, and Busy stays for everyone whose time goes elsewhere.

pairs.distinction: No fun is about play and enjoyment being gone; Busy is about having no time at all.
pairs.reason: Someone can have free hours and still never do anything just for fun, which the first No fun alternative makes explicit.

pairs.distinction: No fun is about not playing at all; Invitations is about wanting company to go out with.
pairs.reason: One is missing enjoyment and the other is missing people to share it with, and a person knows which one is theirs.

pairs.distinction: Paperwork names the forms, bills and hold time; Stress is the general feeling of too much.
pairs.reason: Paperwork is a concrete chore people can point to, while Stress covers being overwhelmed by anything.

pairs.distinction: Legal trouble is one serious problem you can't afford to fix; Paperwork is the steady pile of everyday forms and bills.
pairs.reason: Being stuck in a lawsuit or legal case feels nothing like a week of forms and hold music, so no one would mix them up.

pairs.distinction: Legal trouble is my own legal problem; Justice is seeing courts and police treat people differently.
pairs.reason: One is a personal problem and the other a view about society, so they belong on different pages without a link.

pairs.distinction: Doomscrolling is losing nights to the phone; Focus is not being able to keep your mind on one thing.
pairs.reason: The phone can cause poor focus, but someone who can't concentrate at work and someone who scrolls until 2am each know which they are.

burnout.name: Burnout
burnout.line: Work has worn me down so much that I dread every morning.
burnout.why: Keeps the exhaustion of the original and says what it looks like in a day: dreading the start of work.

burnout.name: Burned out
burnout.line: By the end of the workday I have nothing left for my family or myself.
burnout.why: Keeps 'nothing left' from the original and shows where it lands: the hours after work.

bad-job.name: Mistreated at work
bad-job.line: My boss or coworkers treat me badly, and I dread going in.
bad-job.why: Says it the way a person would and names who does it, while staying one issue.

meaningless-work.name: Pointless work
meaningless-work.line: I spend my days on work that doesn't help anyone.
meaningless-work.why: Names the problem rather than the area, so the heading doesn't mix labels, and makes it something you can picture.

wrong-career.name: Wrong career
wrong-career.line: I'm in the wrong line of work, and I don't know how to switch.
wrong-career.why: Names the problem rather than the area, and the second half separates it from work that merely feels pointless.

pairs.distinction: Unemployment is having no job now; Layoffs is having one and fearing you'll lose it.
pairs.reason: Someone out of work and someone afraid of losing work are in different places and need different help.

pairs.distinction: Unemployment is my own search for work; AI job losses is a worry about what happens to everyone's jobs.
pairs.reason: One is a personal situation today and the other is a societal worry, so people won't confuse them.
Fearing for my own job and worrying that AI will take people's jobs are the same fear seen from the personal and the societal page.

pairs.distinction: Underpaid is about pay that doesn't match the work; Broke is running out of money, which can happen for many reasons.
pairs.reason: Plenty of people are underpaid without running out of money, and plenty run short for reasons other than pay.

pairs.distinction: Mistreatment is how people at work treat me; Burnout is being worn down by the work itself.
pairs.reason: You can burn out under a kind boss and be mistreated without being exhausted, so the two are easy to tell apart.

pairs.distinction: Mistreatment is about how I'm treated; Underpaid is about what I'm paid.
pairs.reason: Low pay and bad treatment often come together, but a person can easily say which one they mean.

pairs.distinction: Meaning is feeling the job doesn't help anyone; Career is being in a field that doesn't fit me and wanting to switch.
pairs.reason: Someone can be in the right field doing pointless tasks, or in the wrong field doing useful work, and the sharper lines in the alternatives make that choice easy.

pairs.distinction: Career is about the work I do now; Direction is not knowing how to reach a goal I already have, in any part of life.
pairs.reason: Direction covers goals well beyond work, while Career is specifically about being in the wrong job.

pairs.distinction: Burnout is being worn down by work; Tired is being tired all the time, often from sleep or health.
pairs.reason: Tiredness has many causes besides work, and burnout is about the job as much as the body.

pairs.distinction: Burnout is having no energy left; Busy is having no hours left.
pairs.reason: A person can have free hours and still be burned out, or be rested but have no time of their own.

no-time-off.name: Time off
no-time-off.line: I never get a real break from work.

sources.passage: Paid vacation leave was available to 80 percent of private industry workers
Some 46% of U.S. workers who receive paid time off from their employer
A similar share (49%) say they'd worry about falling behind at work if they took more time off.

no-time-off.prevalence: Paid vacation was available to 80 percent of U.S. private industry workers (BLS). Of workers who get paid time off, 46% take less than they're offered, and 49% of those say they'd worry about falling behind (Pew).

data.notes: Fifteen lists read. oecd.org returned 403 (also the Better Life Index redirect) and web.archive.org is blocked, so OECD entries are the Work-life balance indicators, with definitions quoted from a Sustainable Brands summary of the OECD index; the gender gap indicator has no passage. The WHOQOL-BREF PDFs loaded but their text could not be extracted, so Q14 has no passage. Gallup Most Important Problem, Ipsos What Worries the World and the WHO/IHME cause-of-burden lists name no time, chores, paperwork, legal or screen-time pain, so they have no entries here. Wikidata QIDs came from the wbsearchentities API (rate-limited; about 20 lookups, not counted as searches). Candidates: no-time-off sits close to the Work group; benefits-runaround overlaps life-admin (Paperwork) and legal-mess. Life-admin has no Wikidata item in the catalog; Q116039772 (paperwork) fits. The rushed and time-crunch figures are old (Pew 2005, Gallup 2015); no newer U.S. series was found. Leads not proposed because no opened list names them: unpredictable shift schedules, waiting on hold, boredom or empty time. Withdrawn at the coordinator's request because the work sweep 20261019-224658 covers them: long-commute (same ID there) and sick-days (near-duplicate of no-paid-leave). Their entries are recorded out of scope. Sources kept: long-commute: https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2021/one-way-travel-time-to-work-rises.html ("the average one-way commute in the United States increased to a new high of 27.6 minutes in 2019"); long-commute: https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2021/one-way-travel-time-to-work-rises.html ("the percentage of workers reporting commutes of 60 minutes or longer increased from 7.9% in 2006 to 9.8% in 2019"); sick-days: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ebs2.nr0.htm ("81 percent had access to paid sick leave"); sick-days: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ebs2.nr0.htm ("Access to paid sick leave for private industry workers ranged from 58 percent for the leisure and hospitality industry").

long-hours.name: Long hours
long-hours.line: I work so many hours that there's barely any of my life left.

sources.passage: 10% of employees in the OECD work 50 hours or more per week in paid work.
745 000 deaths from stroke and ischemic heart disease in 2016
currently stands at 9% of the total population globally

long-hours.prevalence: 10% of employees in OECD countries work 50 hours or more a week; 9% of the world's population works long hours, and long hours caused 745 000 deaths from stroke and heart disease in 2016 (WHO and ILO).

unpredictable-schedule.name: Schedule
unpredictable-schedule.line: My work hours change so often that I can't plan my life.

sources.passage: 60% receive their work schedules less than two weeks in advance; 73% report irregular or variable work schedules; 45% worked consecutive closing/opening shifts (“clopenings”)
2.8 million on-call workers (1.7 percent of total employment)

unpredictable-schedule.prevalence: Among Boston service workers, 60% get their schedules less than two weeks ahead, 73% have irregular or variable schedules and 45% worked a closing shift followed by an opening shift (Shift Project); 2.8 million U.S. workers are on call (1.7 percent of employment, BLS).

unsafe-work.prevalence: U.S. private employers reported 2.5 million nonfatal workplace injuries and illnesses in 2024, and 5,070 people died from work injuries that year (BLS).

wage-theft.name: Wage theft
wage-theft.line: My boss doesn't pay me everything I've earned.

sources.passage: The report says this form of wage theft affects 17 percent of low-wage workers.

wage-theft.prevalence: 17 percent of low-wage workers are paid less than the minimum wage; in the 10 most populous states that is 2.4 million workers losing $8 billion a year (Economic Policy Institute, via Next City).

bad-boss.line: My boss makes my job miserable.

sources.passage: Gallup surveyed over 7,000 members of the US workforce and found that half of them have left a job at some point in their careers solely because they could no longer put up with their manager.

bad-boss.prevalence: Half of more than 7,000 U.S. workers have left a job at some point to get away from their manager (Gallup); 59% are highly satisfied with their relationship with their manager (Pew).

no-say-at-work.name: No say at work
no-say-at-work.line: I have no say in how things are done at work.

sources.passage: 48% of nonunion workers said they would vote for a union if an election was held at their workplace.

overqualified.name: Overqualified

data.notes: Web searches: 21, plus 32 Wikidata wbsearchentities lookups (first attempt rate-limited, retried with backoff). oecd.org returned 403: OECD Jobs and Work-Life Balance indicators read from the Better Life Index mirror (oecd-better-life-index.truth-and-beauty.net). PDFs (OECD slide deck, WHOQOL-BREF scoring PDF, Ipsos monthly PDFs) could not be parsed; WHOQOL item read from an HTML copy, Ipsos from its live page (country figures only). Gallup MIP: 2022 table read from Datawrapper vEKjO CSV. epi.org, migrationpolicy.org, axios.com returned 403: EPI wage-theft figures via Next City, MPI brain-waste figures via the American Immigration Council release. apa.org rendered empty: APA release read on Newswise. 211: no report found ranks employment among top needs; United Way's national snapshot lists income support seventh. WHO/IHME cause-of-burden lists name diseases; the WHO/ILO long-working-hours estimate and BLS injury counts stand in. SDG 8.7 (forced and child labour) again has no pain; flag for fairness or safety. Overlaps for review: bad-boss with bad-job (Mistreatment); long-hours with burnout and no-free-time; unpredictable-schedule with uneven-pay; two-jobs and wage-theft with underpaid and broke; long-commute with getting-around; dead-end-job with stuck and no-path; overqualified with need-skills and wrong-career; gig-work with job-could-go and uneven-pay. Not proposed: age and other discrimination at work (mapped to treated-differently, societal; a personal-page work pain may be worth a refine pass), workplace sexual harassment (mapped to bad-job; a sensitive narrower pain may be worth a refine pass).
